plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 22: Electric Charges and Fields
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic three-dimensional depiction of a hydrogen atom drawn as one large sphere. The sphere is rendered as a grey outline circle with a paler grey ellipse across its middle standing for an equatorial plane, which gives the drawing depth. At the center sits a small dark blue disc bearing a plus sign, representing the proton. A second, much smaller pale blue sphere representing the electron is placed on the upper right of the spherical surface, and a thin blue arc curves down to it from the top of the sphere. A straight black line labeled r joins the central charge to the electron, and a thick red arrow labeled F lies along that same line, pointing from the electron back toward the nucleus. A vertical dashed line through the center, a horizontal dashed line across the equatorial ellipse, and faint blue dashed guides dropping from the electron to that ellipse fix the electron's position in three dimensions. Drawing the force antiparallel to r conveys at a glance that the interaction is attractive and directed along the line joining the two particles. The sketch sets up a Coulomb's law calculation of the force on the ground-state electron at its most probable distance from the proton.

pale gray equatorial ellipse through the sphere center, representing the horizontal mid-plane
vertical black dashed axis passing through the proton and continuing above the sphere
horizontal black dashed axis across the equatorial plane through the proton
short black dashed diagonal/receding axis from the proton toward the lower-left side of the equatorial ellipse
central proton drawn as a small dark blue circular disk or sphere with a white plus sign
electron drawn as a small pale blue sphere on the upper-right quadrant of the spherical guide
thin curved pale blue arc on the spherical surface from the top of the sphere down to the electron
straight black radial segment from the proton to the electron labeled r
thick red force arrow lying along the same radial line and pointing from the electron back toward the proton, labeled F
faint pale blue dashed vertical guide line dropping from the electron to the equatorial plane
faint pale blue dashed guide segment on the equatorial plane from the electron projection foot toward the proton
faint pale blue dashed horizontal guide segment from the electron projection foot toward the right side of the equatorial plane
text label r placed just above the black radial segment near the electron
text label F placed beside the red inward-pointing force arrow

interactions.teaches: The Coulomb force on the electron is always a central attractive force: wherever the electron is placed on the spherical guide, the force arrow points directly back toward the proton along the line joining the two charges

interactions.label: Electron-proton separation r / a₀
interactions.teaches: Changing the separation changes only the magnitude according to the inverse-square law; the force direction remains radial and inward toward the proton

demo_steps.title: Most probable radius
demo_steps.narration: At r = a₀, the electron sits on the upper-right part of the spherical guide. The red force vector is antiparallel to the radius vector, showing attraction toward the proton.

demo_steps.title: Closer electron
demo_steps.narration: Move the electron inward to r = 0.6a₀. The direction is still radial, but the red force arrow grows much longer because the force scales as 1/r².

demo_steps.title: Farther electron
demo_steps.narration: Move the electron outward to r = 2a₀. The same radial geometry remains, but the force arrow becomes shorter as the separation increases.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a nearly front-on orthographic/axonometric composition matching the source: the proton is at the visual center, the sphere appears as a large circle with an equatorial ellipse across the middle. Let the default spherical guide radius be R = 2.0 world units when r/a0 = 1; scale the guide radius linearly with the separation slider, so R = 2.0*(r/a0). The source electron direction is in the upper-right quadrant: use a default unit direction approximately (x=0.48, y=0.70, z=0.53) in world coordinates, with +X screen-right, +Y screen-up, and +Z receding into the page/ellipse depth. Electron position is center + R*direction. Outer sphere outline: light gray #b8b8b8, thin stroke. Equatorial ellipse: light gray #d2d2d2, thin stroke, horizontal major axis about 2R and vertical minor axis about 0.32R in screen projection. Proton: radius about 0.13R, dark blue #1f4f7a with slight highlight; white plus sign centered. Electron: radius about 0.075R, pale blue #77b9cf with darker rim #4e9bb5. Radius segment r: black #111111, thin line from center to electron. Force arrow F: red #c91f2b, thick, collinear with the radius but pointing inward from near the electron toward the proton; visual arrow length should be proportional to 1/(r/a0)^2 but clamped to about 0.25R minimum and 0.9R maximum for readability. Place label r just above the outer half of the black radial segment; place label F beside the red arrow near its middle. Dashed axes are black or dark gray #333333 with dash pattern; vertical axis extends from slightly below center to beyond the sphere top, horizontal axis spans across the equatorial ellipse, diagonal dashed axis goes from center toward the lower-left/rear edge. Pale blue construction guides #78c7df are dashed and thin: vertical drop from electron to its projection on the equatorial plane, then planar guide segments from that foot toward the proton and toward the right side of the ellipse. Coulomb law to encode: |F| = k e^2 / r^2; for display use normalized magnitude |F|/|F(a0)| = 1/(r/a0)^2. Physical constants if shown in optional readout: a0 = 5.29e-11 m, k = 8.99e9 N m²/C², e = 1.602e-19 C, giving |F(a0)| about 8.24e-8 N.
interactionPlan.notes: Implement the sphere as a transparent guide with custom outline curves rather than a shaded solid, to preserve the textbook schematic look. Drag should constrain the electron to the spherical surface at the current radius, updating the black r segment, red inward force arrow, blue surface arc, and dashed projection guides continuously. The separation slider should preserve the current angular direction while moving the electron radially and rescaling the guide sphere and force length. Keep labels billboarding toward the camera so r and F remain readable.

authoredContext:
The Force on the Electron in Hydrogen A hydrogen atom consists of a single proton and a single electron. The proton has a charge of +e and the electron has −e. In the “ground state” of the atom, the electron orbits the proton at most probable distance of 5.29×10−11m (the figure). Calculate the electric force on the electron due to the proton.

A schematic depiction of a hydrogen atom, showing the force on the electron. This depiction is only to enable us to calculate the force; the hydrogen atom does not really look like this. Recall another section.

A positive charge is shown at the center of a sphere of radius r. An electron is depicted as a particle on the sphere. The force on the electron is along the radius, toward the nucleus.

Strategy For the purposes of this example, we are treating the electron and proton as two point particles, each with an electric charge, and we are told the distance between them; we are asked to calculate the force on the electron. We thus use Coulomb’s law.
